item.content:encoded:
Live Forum Statistics

Live Forum Statistics is a powerful, modular, and fully native statistics widget for vBulletin 6 Site Builder, featuring a modern two-column layout, dynamic activity tabs, advanced member rankings, and fully responsive mobile support.

Exclusive release by web-start.net

✨ Key Features ✨
  • Modern Two-Column Layout — Displays forum activity and member rankings in a clean, organized, and responsive design.
  • Dynamic Member Rankings — Switch between Top Posters, Newest Members, and Most Reacted.
  • Cyclic Rank Badges — Attractive ranking badges with dynamically repeating color schemes, supporting any number of displayed rows.
  • Guest-Accessible Rankings — Guests can view member rankings without permission errors.
  • Latest Posts — Displays thread titles, last reply authors, and last post dates, with direct navigation to the latest post.
  • Latest Threads — Shows recently created discussions with author names and discussion statistics.
  • Hottest Threads — Highlights discussions with the highest participation and engagement.
  • Most Viewed Threads — Displays the most frequently viewed discussions.
  • Up to 6 Custom Channel Tabs — Create custom tabs with individual titles and filter discussions by specific channels.
  • Remember Selected Tab — Automatically remembers each visitor's selected tab across page reloads.
  • Independent Auto Refresh — Refreshes widget data automatically without reloading the entire page.
  • Responsive Mobile Design — Automatically adapts the two-column layout for smaller screens.
  • Synchronized Row Alignment — Keeps rows and titles consistently aligned across both columns.




📊 Widget Sections & Features 📊

1. Member Rankings (Sidebar)
  • Top Posters — Displays members with the highest number of posts.
  • Newest Members — Displays the most recently registered members.
  • Most Reacted — Highlights members who have received the most reactions.
  • Dynamic Rank Colors — Ranking badge colors automatically cycle through an attractive color palette, regardless of the number of displayed rows.
  • Guest Access — Member rankings remain accessible to visitors who are not logged in.


2. Forum Activity Tabs
  • Latest Posts — Displays thread titles, last post authors, and posting dates. Clicking a topic takes users directly to its latest post using vBulletin's native post redirection.
  • Latest Threads — Displays the newest discussions along with their authors and activity information.
  • Hottest Threads — Shows discussions with the highest user participation and engagement.
  • Most Viewed — Lists the most viewed discussions across the forum.
  • Custom Channel Tabs (1–6) — Create up to six additional tabs, each with a custom title and a selected forum channel.


3. User Experience & Interaction
  • Remember Selected Tab — Saves the active tab in the visitor's browser and restores it on subsequent page loads.
  • Automatic Refresh — Refreshes widget data independently at configurable intervals: 30 seconds, 1 minute, or 2 minutes.
  • No Full Page Reload — Updates the widget without refreshing the entire forum page.
  • Responsive Layout — Automatically adjusts the widget layout for desktop, tablet, and mobile devices.
  • Consistent Row Alignment — Maintains synchronized row heights and title alignment across both columns.

4.png

1.png

3.png


⚙️ Site Builder Settings ⚙️

The widget includes configurable options directly inside the vBulletin Site Builder live editor. Simply click the widget settings icon to customize its appearance and behavior.
  1. Widget Title — Use the default widget title or enter a custom title.
  2. Left Column List — Select the default ranking category: Top Posters, Newest Members, or Most Reacted.
  3. Rows per Tab — Configure the number of rows displayed in each section (Default: 10).
  4. Auto Refresh — Choose the automatic refresh interval:
    • Never
    • 30 Seconds
    • 1 Minute
    • 2 Minutes
  5. Remember Selected Tab — Enable or disable automatic tab selection memory.
  6. Default Tab Visibility — Independently enable or disable the following tabs:
    • Latest Posts
    • Latest Threads
    • Hottest Threads
    • Most Viewed
  7. Custom Tabs 1–6 — Enable each custom tab, define its display title, and select the associated forum channel using the native channel selector.


🚀 Performance & Technical Architecture 🚀
  • No Database Modifications — Does not create additional database tables or modify the original vBulletin database structure.
  • Clean Installation & Uninstallation — Designed without intrusive database changes or heavy installation routines.
  • Two-Level Instance Caching — Uses vBulletin's internal caching system with a standard 1-minute expiration time to minimize repeated database queries.
  • Native vBulletin 6 APIs — Built using standard vBulletin APIs, including vB_Api_Search, Node libraries, and the vB5_Route routing system.
  • Dark & Light Style Compatibility — Designed to work with different forum styles and display modes.
  • Language Compatibility — All interface labels and text are managed through the native vBulletin Phrase system.
  • RTL & Persian Support — Supports right-to-left layouts and Persian language environments.
  • Mobile Responsive — Automatically adapts to different screen sizes and devices.


📥 Installation & Upgrade 📥
  1. Upload the contents of the
    Code:
    upload
    directory to your vBulletin installation root.
  2. Go to:
    Code:
    AdminCP → Plugins & Products → Manage Products
  3. Click Add/Import Product and select the following XML file:
    Code:
    product_webstartforumstats.xml
  4. Import the product. If upgrading from an earlier version, enable the Overwrite option.
  5. Navigate to your forum homepage or any desired page and enable Site Builder.
  6. Find the web-start category in the widget list.
  7. Drag and drop the Live Forum Statistics widget into your preferred page position.
  8. Save your layout.
  9. Done! Your live forum statistics widget is now ready to use.


🔧 Technical Details 🔧
  • Product ID: webstartforumstats
  • Version: 1.1.1
  • Platform: vBulletin 6
  • Compatibility: vBulletin 6.0.0 to 6.9.9+
  • PHP Requirements: PHP 8.1 / 8.2 / 8.3
  • Integration: Native vBulletin Site Builder Widget
  • Widget Category: web-start
  • Custom Tabs: Up to 6
  • Default Rows: 10
  • Auto Refresh Intervals: 30 Seconds, 1 Minute, 2 Minutes, or Disabled
  • Caching: vBulletin Instance Cache (1 Minute)
  • Database Modifications: None
  • Developer: Web-Start (www.web-start.net)


❓ FAQ ❓
  1. Does this add-on work with vBulletin 5? No. It is designed specifically for vBulletin 6.
  2. Where can I display the widget? Anywhere supported by the native vBulletin Site Builder, including the homepage, channel pages, sidebars, and other widget positions.
  3. Can I customize the widget title? Yes. You can change the title directly through the Site Builder widget settings.
  4. How many custom tabs are supported? Up to six custom channel tabs, each with its own title and channel selection.
  5. Can guests view member rankings? Yes. The ranking sections are accessible to both guests and registered users.
  6. Does automatic refresh reload the entire page? No. Only the widget data is refreshed.
  7. Can I disable individual activity tabs? Yes. You can independently enable or disable each default activity tab.
  8. Does the widget support mobile devices? Yes. The layout automatically adapts to smaller screens.
  9. Does it modify the vBulletin database? No. It does not create additional database tables or modify the original database structure.


🔒 Security & Support 🔒
  • Uses native vBulletin APIs and caching mechanisms.
  • Does not modify the original vBulletin database structure.
  • Designed to minimize unnecessary database queries and server overhead.
  • Back up your database and files before installing or upgrading.
  • For installation assistance or technical support, visit Web Start.

item.content:encoded:
LLMs.txt AI Directory

LLMs.txt AI Directory is a powerful AI SEO add-on for vBulletin 6 that automatically generates standards-compliant llms.txt and llms-full.txt files, helping AI search engines and language models discover, understand, and reference your forum content.

Exclusive release by web-start.net

✨ Key Features ✨
  • Automatically generates structured and standards-compliant llms.txt and llms-full.txt files.
  • Introduces your forum, channels, featured discussions, rules, and feeds to AI crawlers.
  • Helps AI-powered platforms such as Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT Search, Claude, and Perplexity discover your public forum content.
  • Privacy protection — only includes channels and topics accessible to guest users.
  • Excludes private, VIP, restricted, and hidden forum content.
  • Smart BBCode & HTML Stripper — converts forum content into clean Markdown format.
  • Quad-Layer Delivery System — supports dynamic routing, physical file generation, and hybrid delivery.
  • Smart database caching to minimize repeated queries and server load.
  • Automatic scheduled updates without manual intervention.
  • Dedicated AdminCP dashboard with live previews, file health checks, and crawler statistics.
  • Instant file regeneration with a single click.

1.png

2.png




⚙️ Settings & Configuration ⚙️

The add-on provides a comprehensive configuration panel under:

Code:
AdminCP → Settings → Options → Web Start LLMs.txt AI Settings
  1. Enable LLMs.txt Generator — Enable or disable the add-on globally (Default: Enabled).
  2. Site Summary — Define a short description of your forum for AI models (1–3 sentences). Uses the default forum description if left empty.
  3. AI Context & Guidelines — Provide instructions on how AI models should reference your forum content, such as including topic links and author names.
  4. Delivery Mode — Choose how generated files are delivered:
    • Hybrid (Recommended) — Combines dynamic routing and physical file generation.
    • Dynamic Route Only — Serves files directly through vBulletin without creating physical files.
    • Static Physical File Only — Generates and serves physical text files from your hosting root directory.
  5. Cache Lifetime — Configure how often cached database content is refreshed (Default: 24 hours).
  6. Excluded Channel IDs — Exclude specific channels from AI-generated files by entering their channel IDs.
  7. Include Featured Topics — Include selected popular, important, and trending discussions.
  8. Max Topics — Set the maximum number of featured topics (Default: 25).
  9. Enable llms-full.txt — Enable or disable the extended version of the AI directory.


📊 AdminCP Dashboard 📊

A dedicated AI & LLMs.txt Manager dashboard is available in the AdminCP sidebar.
  • File Health Checks — View file status, file sizes, and root directory write permissions.
  • Crawler Statistics — Track the number of requests made by AI crawlers to your generated files.
  • Live Preview — Preview the exact Markdown output served to AI search engines and language models.
  • Rebuild Now — Instantly regenerate the database cache and physical files with a single click.


📥 Installation 📥
  1. Upload the contents of the
    Code:
    upload
    directory included in the package to your vBulletin installation root.
  2. Go to:
    Code:
    AdminCP → Plugins & Products → Manage Products → Add/Import Product
  3. Import the product XML file located at:
    Code:
    core/packages/wsllmstxt/xml/product_wsllmstxt.xml
  4. Set Overwrite to Yes if updating an existing installation.
  5. Navigate to:
    Code:
    AdminCP → Settings → Options → Web Start LLMs.txt AI Settings
  6. Configure your forum description, AI guidelines, delivery mode, and other options.
  7. Visit
    Code:
    https://yourdomain.com/llms.txt
    to verify your generated AI directory.
  8. Done! Your forum is now ready to provide structured content to AI crawlers.


🔧 Technical Details 🔧
  • Product ID: wsllmstxt
  • Version: 1.0.0
  • Compatibility: vBulletin 6.0.0 to 6.9.x+
  • PHP Requirements: PHP 8.1 to 8.3+
  • Developer: Web Start
  • Output Files: llms.txt and llms-full.txt
  • Output Format: Markdown (text/markdown)
  • Caching: Database caching with configurable lifetime
  • Scheduled Updates: Automatic
  • AdminCP Dashboard: Included


❓ FAQ ❓
  1. What is llms.txt? It is a Markdown-based convention designed to provide AI systems with structured information about a website and its content.
  2. Does this add-on expose private forum content? No. Only content accessible to guest users is eligible for inclusion.
  3. What is the difference between llms.txt and llms-full.txt? llms.txt provides a concise overview, while llms-full.txt offers a more comprehensive version with additional topic information.
  4. Does it support ChatGPT and Perplexity? The generated files provide structured content that AI-powered search and language-model systems can discover and potentially use.
  5. Does it affect forum performance? Database caching and physical file delivery options are designed to minimize repeated database queries and PHP processing.
  6. Can I exclude specific channels? Yes. Enter the channel IDs in the Excluded Channel IDs setting.
  7. Can I regenerate the files manually? Yes. Use the Rebuild Now button in the AdminCP dashboard.


🔒 Security & Support 🔒
  • Only guest-accessible public content is included in generated files.
  • Private, restricted, and VIP channel content is excluded.
  • Database caching helps reduce unnecessary server queries.
  • Always back up your database and files before installing or updating.
  • For installation assistance or technical support, visit Web Start.

item.title: vBulletin 7 — Technical Proposal
item.description:
vBulletin 7 — Technical Proposal
Summary
We propose that vBulletin 7 is a deliberate modernization of the existing core, not a rewrite: a slimmer, faster, file-based platform on Symfony...
item.content:encoded:
vBulletin 7 — Technical Proposal



Summary

We propose that vBulletin 7 is a deliberate modernization of the existing core, not a rewrite: a slimmer, faster, file-based platform on Symfony components, with a brand-new extension system, Twig templates, file-based languages and a light frontend.

The current architecture (a presentation app that calls an internal API, with routes, libraries and data managers behind it) is sound. What holds us back is the weight that has piled up around it: no namespaces, a service locator instead of dependency injection, PHP code stored in XML and run through eval(), a 3.5 MB style file, a 2019 editor, and 600 KB of JavaScript on every page.

If we fix those things and ship only when v7 is measurably faster and more complete than 6.x, we can offer a combination few forum platforms offer today:
  • Everything in the box. Forums, blogs, groups, albums, articles and calendar built in, each one optional.
  • The best developer experience of any forum platform. A typed API, a CLI that scaffolds extensions, and docs written so that both people and AI assistants can build add-ons in an hour.
  • Painless migration from other forum platforms, with URLs and passwords preserved.


Old 6.x add-ons will not run on v7. We accept that on purpose: the add-on ecosystem has already thinned out, and a clean break is what lets us remove eval(), XML-embedded code and the global registry for good. Forum data, users and URLs always carry over.

Where 6.2.3 stands today

The core is in better shape than its reputation, but almost none of it follows the conventions a PHP developer expects in 2026. Every number below was measured directly on the 6.2.3 package, with vb.phar and libraries.phar extracted and the code counted with PHP's own tokenizer.

What is already good
  • Sound layering. index.php routes through the vB5_Frontend_* app, which calls the core API in-process (includes/api/interface/collapsed.php). Routes, API, libraries and data managers are cleanly separated.
  • One query layer. Almost all SQL goes through the assertor and named queries (querydefs.php: 95 table definitions, 219 named and 93 method queries). There are only 3 inline SQL strings inside the core.
  • Modern password hashing. argon2id and bcrypt are used, with the legacy md5 scheme kept only to rehash old accounts. CSRF tokens are in place.
  • Current server baseline. The minimums are PHP 8.2, MySQL 8.0.11 and MariaDB 10.6.
  • Current Composer packages. Inside libraries.phar: Guzzle 7.10, PHPMailer 7.0, ramsey/uuid 4.9, league/oauth2-client 2.9 and others.
  • The start of an extension model. core/packages/<name>/ already holds product.php, hooks.php, api/ and library/. vB_Api_Wrapper also runs extension classes after every API call.


What holds us back
Area Measured fact Why it matters
Code style 887 first-party PHP files (519 inside a minified vb.phar). 0 namespaces, 0 strict_types, no test suite Unfamiliar to modern PHP developers. Stack traces point at 65,000-character lines
Typing 17% of 5,246 methods have return types; 19% of properties are typed IDEs and static analysis can do little
Dependencies vB::getDbAssertor() 811×, getDatastore() 562×, getUserContext() 421×. Legacy $vbulletin registry in 106 files No DI container. Hard to test or to replace a service
Procedural code core/includes: 41,000 lines, 387 global functions. AdminCP: 52,000 lines, 3,553 print_* calls Slow to change. AdminCP looks and feels dated
Code execution 23 eval() calls: template runtime, product install and uninstall code, setting validation Security and debugging risk. Add-on code lives in the database
Add-on packaging Templates, phrases, settings and install code ship in one XML per product Hard to review, diff or version with Git
Styles and language Master style: 598 templates and 1,082 stylevars in a 3.5 MB XML. 10,621 phrases in a 1.8 MB XML Designers and translators can't work in files
Editor CKEditor 4.13.0 (2019). CKEditor 4 is end-of-life Highest-priority security item
Frontend weight Every public page loads jQuery (88 KB) plus footer-rollup.js (514 KB, 148 KB gzip): jQuery UI 1.13, qtip, jCarousel (2018), history.js and others Poor Core Web Vitals on mobile
Database node has 57 columns and 32 indexes. Several time columns are signed INT. 3 tables are still MyISAM Every new post updates 32 indexes. Y2038 limit
Dead or old code APC cache backend (APC no longer exists on PHP 7+). Facebook PHP SDK 4.0.9 (abandoned). Stripe PHP 8.8.0 Maintenance cost and risk
Upgrade path 369 upgrade step classes, 52,854 lines, going back to vB 3.5 A large surface we keep maintaining
Migration No importer from other platforms in core (bulkimporter.php is a vB4 CMS upgrade helper) No path for sites on other platforms to move to vBulletin
YUI is used only in AdminCP and the installer, not on public pages.

Goals and release targets

v7 ships as Final only when it meets every target below, measured on the same hardware and data as 6.2.x. These are proposed numbers for the team to confirm, not measurements.

Product goals
  1. Be the fastest full-featured forum platform. A thread page should feel instant on a mid-range phone.
  2. Make writing an extension a one-hour job for a PHP developer, or for an AI assistant following our docs.
  3. Let a site on another forum platform move to vBulletin in an afternoon without losing URLs, users or search ranking.
  4. Keep the "everything in the box" promise, but make every large feature optional.


Release gate (proposed targets)
Metric Target for 7.0 Final How we measure
JavaScript on a thread page ≤ 50 KB gzip (editor loaded only when the reply box opens) Lighthouse and the network panel on a default install
CSS on a thread page ≤ 30 KB gzip Same
DB queries per thread page ≤ 15 for a guest, ≤ 20 for a member Built-in query explain mode (vB5_Frontend_ExplainQueries)
Server time to first byte ≤ 100 ms on shared-hosting class hardware, warm cache Benchmark script with 1M posts
Lighthouse mobile performance ≥ 95 on index, forum and thread pages Lighthouse CI in the build
Core Web Vitals LCP < 2.0 s, INP < 200 ms, CLS < 0.05 Lighthouse and field data from beta sites
eval() calls in core 0 CI grep check
Code with namespaces and strict_types 100% of new code; 100% of core classes behind PSR-4 aliases PHPStan in CI
Static analysis PHPStan level 6 or higher on new code CI
Test coverage of the API layer ≥ 60% of public API methods have tests PHPUnit in CI
Upgrade from 5.7.x / 6.x Completes without manual steps on the test data set Upgrade CI job
Official extensions available 15 or more covering the most-requested add-ons Marketplace list
Principles

v7 keeps the data and the URLs, and breaks the code interfaces once, cleanly.

What we keep
  • Every site's data: users, nodes, permissions, attachments, settings and phrases.
  • Every public URL, or a permanent 301 redirect to its new form.
  • The layering of routes, API, libraries and data managers, and the assertor with named queries.
  • The "everything in the box" feature set, repackaged as official extensions.


What we break, on purpose
  • Old XML products, PHP hook code stored in the database, and {vb:...} templates in custom styles. A converter handles the common cases (see Templates and Migration).
  • Global functions and the $vbulletin registry as a public API. They remain only as internal shims during 7.x.
  • PHP below 8.3, so that v7 can rely on typed class constants, readonly classes and current Symfony LTS.


Lessons from vB5 we commit to
  1. No release before parity. 7.0 Final does not ship with fewer features or slower pages than 6.x. A long public beta comes first.
  2. Strangler, not big bang. Every phase leaves a working product. New code wraps old code, then replaces it.
  3. Measured, not claimed. The release gate above runs in CI. Performance numbers in announcements come from the same benchmark.
  4. Developers first. If it is not documented with a working example, it is not finished.
  5. One way to do each thing. Add-ons get one extension format, one event system and one template engine, not two in parallel.


Target architecture

v7 keeps today's layering and puts a small Symfony-component kernel and a real DI container underneath it. We do not adopt a full-stack framework.

Every request passes the same thin layers; extensions plug into each
  1. Entry points — index.php · api.php (REST) · bin/vb console: install, upgrade, cron
  2. Kernel — HttpFoundation · Routing · DI container · session, CSRF, rate limit
  3. Presentation — Controllers render Twig views; page-builder widgets are optional
  4. Core API (the public contract) — vBulletin\Api\*: permissions, validation; what extensions and apps call
  5. Domain libraries — vBulletin\Library\*: business rules; emits typed events (PostCreated)
  6. Infrastructure — Assertor queries · Redis/APCu cache · queue · mailer · search

Extensions plug into every layer above: extension.json manifest · own routes and controllers · Twig templates and slots · service decorators · event subscribers · migrations and queue jobs · CLI commands. Only via vBulletin\Contracts, never internal classes.

The Core API is the one contract that extensions, the mobile app and the REST API depend on. Everything below it may change between minor versions.

Why components, not a full framework

vBulletin is installed by thousands of customers on hosts we don't control, and it must stay stable for years. A full framework would tie our release cycle to theirs. Laravel in particular ships a major version every year. Our own route, API and library layers already do the job of a framework's application layer.

Symfony components give us standard, well-documented building blocks with long-term-support releases. Developers who know Symfony or Laravel recognise them immediately, and several major PHP projects are built the same way.

Components we adopt
Component Replaces in 6.x What it gives us
symfony/dependency-injection vB::getX() service locator (2,500+ calls) Constructor injection, testable services, extensions can decorate any service. Compiled container, no runtime cost
symfony/event-dispatcher vB::getHooks() (26 untyped hooks) and DB-stored hook code Typed events with priorities, the standard PSR-14 model
symfony/console Browser-only installer, upgrader and cron bin/vb install, upgrade, cron:run, cache:clear, make:extension, extension:install
symfony/http-foundation + routing vB5_Frontend_Routing, raw superglobals (1,764 direct uses) Standard request and response objects. Routes from PHP attributes or files, cached
symfony/messenger Heavy cron jobs and synchronous mail and push Background queue (DB transport by default, Redis optional) for mail, notifications, counters and search indexing
symfony/cache Custom cache classes, including dead APC PSR-6/16 caches on Redis, APCu, Memcached and filesystem
symfony/mailer Direct PHPMailer wrapper Transports, templated mail, async sending via Messenger
symfony/rate-limiter, security-csrf Hand-written flood and token checks Tested implementations
twig/twig {vb:...} compiler and eval() runtime See Templates
doctrine/migrations Upgrade step classes for schema changes Versioned schema changes for core and every extension
We do not adopt Doctrine ORM. The assertor and named queries work well and give us full control over SQL on large boards.

Compatibility bridge

During 7.x, vB::getDbAssertor() and the other locator methods remain, but they read from the container. Old internal code keeps working while new code uses constructor injection. Each class moves under a namespace (vB_Api_Node becomes vBulletin\Api\Node) with a class_alias for the old name, so the change can land file by file.

Directory layout

Code:
bin/vb                      # console entry point
config/                     # config.php, services.php, routes
public/                     # index.php, api.php, built assets (web root)
src/
  Api/  Library/  Entity/  Controller/  Event/  Contracts/
  Kernel/  Db/  Search/  Template/  Console/
migrations/                 # core schema migrations
templates/                  # core Twig templates (overridable)
language/en/*.php           # core phrases by group
styles/default/  styles/classic/
extensions/<vendor>/<name>/ # installed extensions
var/cache/  var/log/  var/storage/   # writable, outside the web root
vendor/                     # Composer dependencies (shipped pre-built)
The web root becomes public/, so source, config and storage are no longer reachable over HTTP by accident.

Distribution
  • Source ships unminified and readable. Opcache removes any speed difference, and readable stack traces matter for every add-on developer.
  • vendor/ ships pre-built so shared-hosting customers never need to run Composer. Core dependencies are prefixed with php-scoper (for example vBulletin\Vendor\GuzzleHttp), so an extension can bring its own version of a library without a conflict.
  • The minimum is PHP 8.3, so we can use typed class constants, readonly classes and the current Symfony LTS.


Extension system

An extension in v7 is a folder of ordinary files: PHP classes, Twig templates, phrase files and migrations, described by one extension.json. Nothing is stored as code in the database and nothing runs through eval(). It grows out of what core/packages/ already does; it is not a new invention.

Folder structure

Code:
extensions/acme/seo/
  extension.json            # identity, versions, requirements
  composer.json             # optional: the extension's own dependencies
  src/                      # PSR-4, namespace Acme\Seo\
    Setup.php               # optional install / upgrade / uninstall steps
    Listener/ThreadListener.php
    Controller/SitemapController.php
    Api/SeoApi.php          # optional: adds methods to the public API
  config/
    services.php            # service registration and decorators
    routes.php              # the extension's own routes
    settings.php            # AdminCP settings, with types and defaults
    permissions.php         # new permissions, with defaults per usergroup
  templates/                # Twig: own templates and slot fills
  language/en/seo.php       # phrases
  migrations/               # Doctrine migrations for its own tables
  assets/                   # JS and CSS, built by Vite
  tests/
The manifest

Code:
{
  "id": "acme/seo",
  "name": "SEO Toolkit",
  "version": "1.2.0",
  "description": "Schema.org markup, IndexNow and sitemap tools",
  "author": { "name": "Acme", "url": "https://acme.example" },
  "requires": {
    "vbulletin": "^7.0",
    "php": ">=8.3",
    "extensions": { "vbulletin/blog": "^7.0" }
  },
  "autoload": { "psr-4": { "Acme\\Seo\\": "src/" } },
  "setup": "Acme\\Seo\\Setup",
  "admin": { "settingsGroup": "seo", "icon": "search" }
}
Versions follow semantic versioning. The installer refuses an extension whose requires cannot be met, and it explains why in plain words.

How an extension changes behaviour

There are five sanctioned ways, from lightest to heaviest:
  1. Listen to an event. Typed event objects, for example PostCreated, ThreadViewing, UserRegistered, PermissionsResolving and PostRendering. Listeners are registered in services.php or with a PHP attribute.
  2. Fill a template slot. Core templates declare named slots ({% slot 'thread.after_title' %}). An extension adds a Twig file into a slot without touching the core template. Today's 71 {vb:hook} locations become the first set of slots.
  3. Decorate a service. An extension can wrap any service in the container (for example the search service or the notification sender). This is the clean version of what vB_Api_Extensions does today after each API call.
  4. Add routes, controllers, API methods and CLI commands of its own.
  5. Override a template in a style, the same way a theme does.


There is no sanctioned way to patch core files. If a common need can only be met by patching, that is a missing event or slot, and we add one.

The stability promise
  • Extensions may only depend on interfaces and classes in vBulletin\Contracts\*, events in vBulletin\Event\* and the public API. These are covered by semantic versioning: no breaking change within 7.x.
  • Everything else is internal and marked @internal. PHPStan rules warn extension authors who use it.
  • Deprecations are announced one minor version ahead and logged at runtime in debug mode.


Lifecycle
Step What happens
Install Requirements checked, migrations run, settings and permissions registered with defaults, Setup::install() called, caches rebuilt
Enable / disable The extension's services, routes, listeners and slots are added to or removed from the compiled container. Its data stays
Upgrade New migrations run in order, then Setup::upgrade($from)
Uninstall Setup::uninstall(), migrations rolled back if the admin chooses to remove data, phrases and settings removed
Failure If an extension throws during a request in production, it is logged and that listener or slot is skipped. The page still renders. Repeated failures auto-disable it and notify the admin
Tooling
  • bin/vb make:extension acme/seo creates a working skeleton with a listener, a slot fill, a setting, a phrase, a migration and a test.
  • bin/vb make:listener, make:controller, make:migration, make:setting.
  • bin/vb extension:validate checks the manifest, the namespaces and use of internal classes, and runs the extension's tests.
  • bin/vb extension:package builds a signed zip for the marketplace.
  • In debug mode, template and phrase changes are picked up without rebuilding anything.


Documentation built for people and AI assistants

Every event, slot, contract and setting type is documented from the code itself and published as a website, plus a single llms.txt and machine-readable JSON. A developer, or an AI coding assistant pointed at those docs, should be able to build a correct extension on the first try. No forum platform offers this today, and it lowers the cost of rebuilding our add-on ecosystem.

Templates, styles and languages

In v7, templates, styles and phrases live in files, one per thing, under Git. The database only stores an admin's overrides. This replaces the 3.5 MB style XML, the 1.8 MB language XML and the eval() template runtime.

Template engine: Twig

We move to Twig 3 in 7.0. While the add-on ecosystem is thin, this is the cheapest moment for the change:
  • Designers who have worked with Symfony, Drupal or Craft already know it, and every editor has Twig support.
  • It compiles to PHP class files cached in var/cache/twig, run by opcache. Nothing goes through eval().
  • It escapes output by default, which removes a whole class of XSS mistakes in custom styles.
  • It is sandboxable, so we can safely allow template editing in AdminCP.


The 598 master templates are ported by a converter that handles the regular constructs ({vb:raw}, {vb:var}, {vb:if}, {vb:each}, {vb:phrase}, {vb:url}, {vb:template}) and flags the rest for a person. The same converter is offered to customers for their custom styles, with a report of what it could not convert.

Style structure

Code:
styles/default/
  style.json               # name, parent style, version, preview image
  tokens.css               # design tokens as CSS custom properties
  templates/
    layout/base.twig  layout/header.twig  layout/footer.twig
    forum/index.twig  forum/channel.twig  forum/thread.twig
    components/post.twig  components/pagination.twig  ...
  assets/                  # style-specific CSS and images
  • Inheritance: a child style lists a parent in style.json and contains only the files it changes. Twig resolves a template from child to parent to core.
  • Stylevars become design tokens: the 1,082 stylevars collapse into a much smaller set of CSS custom properties (colours, spacing, radius, fonts) in tokens.css. AdminCP gets a visual editor that writes these tokens, including a dark-mode set. Only a token change rebuilds CSS; there is no per-request stylesheet generation.
  • Admin edits: editing a template in AdminCP stores an override in the database, shown as a diff against the file. An upgrade shows exactly which overridden templates changed upstream, with a three-way merge.
  • Two default styles: "Default" (modern, fast, mobile-first) and "Classic" (the familiar 3.8 / 4.x layout, rebuilt on the same templates). Classic is cheap to build on shared templates and gives long-time members a familiar home.


Languages

Code:
language/en/
  global.php   forum.php   user.php   admin/settings.php   admin/users.php   ...
language/fa/
  global.php   ...
  • Each file returns a PHP array of key => text, compiled into one cached file per language and group, so a page loads only the groups it uses.
  • The 10,621 phrases are split automatically along the existing 62 phrase types.
  • Translations can be exchanged as standard XLIFF or PO files, so translators can use Crowdin, Weblate or POEditor. A public translation project replaces emailing XML files around.
  • ICU message format handles plurals and genders correctly in every language, which also matters for right-to-left languages such as Persian and Arabic.
  • Admin edits to phrases are stored as overrides, exactly like templates.


Database and performance

We keep the node model and the assertor, and we make them cheaper: measure first, then cut index and write cost, move slow work to a queue, and cache whole pages for guests.

Step 1: measure before we change anything

We build a benchmark data set (1M posts, 50k users, 200 channels; plus 10M posts for large-board tests) and a script that records, for the index, channel, thread, profile and search pages: queries, time per query, peak memory and time to first byte. vB5_Frontend_ExplainQueries already gives most of this. The numbers go into CI so that every change shows its effect. The steps below are hypotheses until this data confirms them.

Step 2: the node table
  • node has 57 columns and 32 indexes. Every new post writes all of them, plus one closure row per ancestor. We review each index against real query plans and drop those no query uses. nodeid (nodeid, contenttypeid) next to the primary key, and single-column indexes on low-cardinality flags (sticky, approved, inlist, featured, showpublished), are the first candidates.
  • Rarely-read columns (taglist, deletereason, CRC32, Q&A answer fields) move to a side table, so the hot row stays small.
  • Time columns move to INT UNSIGNED or BIGINT. node.created, node.publishdate and closure.publishdate are signed INT today and stop working in January 2038.
  • The three MyISAM tables (language, phrase, userfield) move to InnoDB. phrase and language largely leave the database anyway with file-based languages.


Step 3: move slow work out of the request

With Symfony Messenger, the work that does not need to happen before the page returns runs in a background worker: counter and last-post updates on parent channels, notification fan-out, email and push, search indexing, related-topics and trending calculation (today's heaviest cron jobs), and thumbnail generation.

On shared hosting the queue drains at the end of requests and from cron. Where a worker is possible, bin/vb messenger:consume runs it continuously.

Step 4: caching
  • Guest full-page cache. Guests are the majority of traffic on most boards and see identical pages. A thread page for a guest is rendered once and served from cache until something in it changes, invalidated by the same events extensions listen to. This alone can take most guest load off PHP and MySQL.
  • Object cache on Redis or APCu (Memcached still supported) for permissions, settings, routes and user info, through symfony/cache. The database cache backend remains the fallback for hosts with nothing else.
  • HTTP caching headers and ETags on pages, attachments and assets, so a CDN or reverse proxy can help out of the box.


Step 5: the heaviest queries

By JOIN count the heaviest query builders are fetchUserinfo (up to 22 conditional JOINs), getFollowingContent (20), getFollowing (18) and fetchProfileMedia (13). Most JOINs are optional, so the real cost depends on the call. The benchmark tells us which ones actually run on hot pages; those get split into smaller cached lookups.

Search

Core keeps the built-in MySQL search for small boards. Search becomes a contract (vBulletin\Contracts\Search\Engine) with official extensions for Meilisearch and OpenSearch/Elasticsearch, and the existing Sphinx support as a community extension. Indexing runs through the queue.

Frontend and editor

The public frontend becomes server-rendered HTML with a small layer of modern JavaScript, loaded per page. The editor is replaced. Together these are the biggest visible wins of v7.

JavaScript
  • Today: every public page loads jQuery (88 KB) and footer-rollup.js (514 KB, 148 KB gzip). That is 37 scripts, including jQuery UI, qtip, jCarousel (last released 2018), history.js and selectBox, whether the page uses them or not.
  • v7: no jQuery on public pages. Interactivity uses small ES modules plus htmx for partial page updates (load more posts, inline edit, reactions, moderation actions) and Alpine.js for local UI state (menus, dialogs, tabs). Both are tiny, need no build step to use, and keep the server as the single source of truth.
  • Build: Vite produces one small shared bundle plus a bundle per page type, with hashed filenames for long-term caching. This replaces jsrollup_vbulletin.xml and cssrollup_vbulletin.xml.
  • Native over plugins: <dialog>, <details>, popover, <input type="date">, CSS scroll-snap and the View Transitions API replace jQuery UI, qtip, jCarousel, history.js and the datepicker.
  • Navigation: View Transitions plus htmx-boosted links give app-like page changes without a single-page-app rewrite. Search engines still get full HTML.
  • AdminCP keeps jQuery during 7.0 so the panel can be ported screen by screen. YUI is removed from AdminCP in 7.0.


CSS
  • One small base stylesheet built from design tokens, plus component CSS loaded with its page.
  • Critical CSS inlined for the first paint; the rest loaded without blocking.
  • Dark mode from the token set, honouring the visitor's system setting.
  • Logical properties (margin-inline-start and so on), so right-to-left languages work without a separate stylesheet.


Editor

CKEditor 4.13.0 (2019) is replaced. CKEditor 4 is end-of-life and no longer receives public security fixes. That makes it the most urgent security item in this proposal.

Proposal: Tiptap (built on ProseMirror). It is modular, headless and easy to extend, which suits an editor that add-ons need to build on.
  • It is loaded only when the reply box gains focus, so it never weighs on reading.
  • It stores a structured document and renders to BBCode for full compatibility with existing posts. Markdown shortcuts while typing (**bold**, > quote, - list) give modern users what they expect.
  • Mentions, quotes, attachments with drag-and-drop and paste, image resize, code blocks with highlighting, tables, spoilers and emoji are built as Tiptap extensions. Add-on authors can add their own buttons and blocks through a documented editor API.
  • An excellent mobile experience is a requirement, not an afterthought.


A security patch for 6.x comes first, by replacing or patching CKEditor in a 6.2.x release, independent of v7 (see Roadmap).

Accessibility

Target WCAG 2.2 AA for the default styles: keyboard navigation everywhere, focus states, labelled controls, correct heading structure and colour contrast checked in CI.

Slim core, official extensions

The v7 core contains only what every community needs. Everything else becomes an official, first-party extension that ships in the download, is maintained by us, and can be switched on in one click. We keep the "everything in the box" promise, but a fresh install is small, fast and simple.

This also proves the extension system: if our own blog, groups and calendar can be built as extensions, any outside developer can build anything.
Feature v7 home On by default
Forums, channels, topics, replies, polls, attachments Core Yes
Users, usergroups, permissions, profiles, registration and login Core Yes
Private messages, notifications, subscriptions Core Yes
Moderation, reports, infractions, warnings, spam protection Core Yes
Search (built-in MySQL engine) Core Yes
Reactions and reputation Core Yes
Blogs Official extension No
Social groups Official extension No
Articles / CMS Official extension No
Calendar and events Official extension No
Photo albums and media gallery Official extension No
Q&A (accepted answers) Official extension No
Paid subscriptions and payment gateways (Stripe, PayPal, Square) Official extension No
PM chat (real-time) Official extension No
Page builder (screen layouts and widgets) Official extension for custom pages; core pages render directly Custom pages only
Google, WordPress, Microsoft and Facebook login Official extensions (OAuth2 via league/oauth2-client) No
Shopify, Nativo, VigLink Official extensions No
Meilisearch and OpenSearch search Official extensions No
Sphinx search Community extension (no longer maintained by us) No
vB4 API compatibility layer (31 files, 210 KB) Removed; the mobile app moves to the new REST API n/a
The page builder

The page builder is a real strength for customers who build portals, but it is also the reason a simple thread page assembles screen layouts and widget instances on every request. In v7, the core pages (index, channel, thread, profile, search) render directly from Twig templates. The page builder remains available for custom pages and for sidebars, through a template slot. Customers who rely on it keep their layouts; everyone else stops paying for it.

Security

v7 removes the structural risks we found in 6.2.3 and makes the safe path the default path for us and for extension authors.
Area 6.2.3 today v7
Code execution 23 eval() calls, including product install code, setting validation and the template runtime Zero. Code lives in files; templates compile to cached PHP classes. CI fails on any eval()
Editor CKEditor 4.13.0 (2019, end-of-life) Tiptap, kept current (see Frontend)
Template output Escaping depends on using {vb:var} vs {vb:raw} correctly Twig auto-escaping; raw output must be explicit and is flagged in review
Serialized data 171 unserialize() calls, 3 with allowed_classes; unserialize_callback_func set to autoload (vb.php:240) Stored structures move to JSON. Remaining unserialize() calls pass allowed_classes => false. The autoload callback is removed
Request input 1,764 direct reads of $_GET / $_POST / $_REQUEST / $_COOKIE across the code One Request object; typed, validated input objects for controllers and API methods
Outdated SDKs Facebook PHP SDK 4.0.9 (abandoned), Stripe PHP 8.8.0, both outside Composer All third-party code through Composer, scoped, with automated advisories (composer audit) in CI
Web root The whole install is web-accessible Only public/ is web-accessible; config, source, cache and logs sit outside it
Small issues e.g. index.php reads $_SERVER['HTTP_USER_AGENT'] without checking it exists Caught by PHPStan at level 6
Additional measures
  • Content Security Policy with nonces, enabled by default on the new frontend. No inline scripts in core templates.
  • Security headers by default: HSTS when on HTTPS, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy.
  • Sessions: SameSite=Lax, HttpOnly and Secure cookies; session rotation on login and privilege change.
  • Accounts: passkeys (WebAuthn) and TOTP two-factor in core; argon2id stays the default hash; rate limits on login, registration, password reset and posting through symfony/rate-limiter.
  • Uploads: stored outside the web root, served through a controller, with type checked by content (not extension) and image re-encoding to strip embedded payloads.
  • Extensions: the marketplace runs automated checks (no eval, no internal classes, no raw SQL from request input) and signs packages. AdminCP warns when installing an unsigned extension.
  • Process: a public security policy and disclosure address, and an advisory for every security release. An external audit before 7.0 Final.


Where v7 stands out

Catching up is not enough; v7 needs clear reasons to choose it. These are the areas where v7 can lead.
  1. Everything in the box. vBulletin already has blogs, groups, albums, articles and a calendar. In v7 they become fast, optional official extensions.
  2. The best developer experience of any forum platform. A typed public API, a stable contracts package, bin/vb make:extension, hot-reloading templates in debug mode, PHPStan rules for extension authors, an OpenAPI description of the REST API, and docs written for both people and AI coding assistants (llms.txt). The pitch to developers: "build your first vBulletin extension in an hour."
  3. A complete REST API and webhooks. Every action a member or moderator can take is available over a versioned, OAuth2-protected REST API, with outgoing webhooks for events. Headless front ends, mobile apps, Discord and Slack bridges and automation tools (Zapier, n8n) can all build on it. This replaces the vB4 compatibility layer.
  4. Real-time by default. New replies, reactions, typing indicators and notifications arrive live through Server-Sent Events with the Mercure protocol, with a polling fallback on shared hosting.
  5. SEO for how search works now. Search engines give forum discussions their own prominent results. v7 ships DiscussionForumPosting structured data, clean canonical URLs, IndexNow pings, fast pages and correct pagination out of the box, with no add-on needed.
  6. Built-in, private-by-default AI assistance (optional). Thread summaries for long discussions, duplicate-question detection when posting, spam and toxicity scoring for moderators, and smart related topics. The admin brings their own provider key or uses a local model; nothing is sent anywhere unless the admin turns it on.
  7. Federation (official extension, 7.x). ActivityPub support, so people on Mastodon and other fediverse platforms can follow and reply to topics. Discussions get discovered outside the forum without depending on one social network.
  8. Migration as a first-class feature. Importers from the most widely used forum platforms, with URL redirects and password-hash compatibility (see Migration). Switching to vBulletin should be easier than switching away.
  9. Classic and modern in one product. A modern default style and a "Classic" style that brings back the 3.8 / 4.x look many long-time admins and members still miss.
  10. Easy hosting. An official Docker image, one-command install (bin/vb install), a Softaculous / Installatron package for shared hosting, and a health page in AdminCP that explains what to fix.
  11. Community-owner tools. Built-in onboarding for new members, scheduled posts, member badges and achievements, and an analytics dashboard (active members, retention, top content). These are what admins measure their success by.


Migration

Two paths matter: our own customers moving up to v7, and sites on other platforms moving over. Both must keep every URL and every member's ability to log in.

From vBulletin 5.x and 6.x
  • Supported starting point: 5.7.x or any 6.x. Older sites (3.x, 4.x, early 5.x) first upgrade to 6.2 with the existing upgrader, then to 7. The 369 historic upgrade step classes (52,854 lines) stay in 6.x and leave the v7 codebase.
  • How it runs: bin/vb upgrade from the command line, with resumable steps, progress output and a dry-run mode that reports problems before any change. The browser upgrader remains for shared hosting and calls the same steps.
  • Data: schema changes are Doctrine migrations, and large tables are migrated in batches so a 10M-post board can upgrade without hours of downtime.
  • Styles: custom templates go through the {vb:...} to Twig converter. The site switches to the new default style automatically, and the converted custom style is offered for review with a list of templates that need a person.
  • Phrases and settings carry over; customised phrases become overrides.
  • Add-ons: v7 lists every installed 6.x product, says whether an official or marketplace replacement exists, and disables the rest. Their data tables are left untouched.
  • URLs: route structures stay the same. Where a route changes (for example removed vB4 API endpoints), a permanent redirect map is generated.


From other platforms

Today no importer from another platform ships in core. In v7 this becomes an official tool, bin/vb import <platform>, with a web wizard on top.
Source Priority Notes
XenForo 2.x 1 Modern schema; reactions and attachments map closely
phpBB 3.3 1 Simple schema; BBCode posts map directly
SMF 2.x, MyBB 1.8 2 Long tail of older communities
Discourse 2 Markdown posts and categories; via its API or a database export
Invision Community 3 Rich content model; attachments need careful mapping
vBulletin 3.x / 4.x direct 3 Many old boards are still online; replaces the separate ImpEx tool
Every importer must:
  1. Import users, groups, permissions as closely as the models allow, forums, topics, posts, polls, attachments, avatars, private messages, likes, tags and moderation history.
  2. Keep passwords working. Store the original hash with its scheme. On a member's first login it is verified with the source platform's algorithm and transparently re-hashed with argon2id. vBulletin's password schemes (pwschemes_vbulletin.xml) already support this pattern.
  3. Keep URLs working. Generate a redirect map from every old URL pattern (topic, post, forum, member and attachment) to the new one, served as permanent 301 redirects, so search ranking carries over.
  4. Run incrementally: import once, keep the old site live, re-sync the delta, then switch DNS. A two-hour cut-over window for a large board should be realistic.
  5. Produce a report: counts per entity on both sides, and anything skipped and why.


We recommend a step-by-step guide for each supported platform, and test migrations of a few large real boards during the beta to harden the importers.

Ecosystem, developer experience and community

Code quality brings developers back, and developers bring add-ons. Add-ons and visible momentum bring admins back. This part of the plan matters as much as the code.

Rebuild the add-on catalogue before launch
  • Launch with 15 or more extensions. Besides our own official extensions (Slim core), we build, or help developers build, the add-ons admins ask for most: advanced SEO, anti-spam (Akismet, StopForumSpam, Turnstile and hCaptcha), thanks / likes leaderboards, member badges, an ads manager, a donation and fundraising widget, a Discord bridge, a link-preview tool, a sitemap and IndexNow tool, a backup tool and a GDPR toolkit.
  • Early-access programme. Six months before 7.0 Final, selected developers get access to betas, a private channel with the core team, and early marketplace placement.
  • Porting support for the most popular 5.x / 6.x add-ons whose authors are still active.


Marketplace
  • Hosted on vbulletin.com with listings, versions, reviews, screenshots and compatibility badges.
  • Install and update from inside AdminCP, verified by package signature.
  • Automated validation on upload (see Security), plus manual review for the "Verified" badge.


Visibility and process
  • Public roadmap and changelog. Regular, predictable releases, for example a minor release every 8 to 10 weeks.
  • Visible team. Core developers post development diaries on vbulletin.com: what is being built, why, with screenshots and code.
  • RFCs for big changes. Significant changes to contracts, events or templates are proposed publicly and discussed before they land.


Documentation
  • A developer guide with a full tutorial (build a real extension end to end), a reference generated from the code (every event, slot, contract, setting type, API endpoint and CLI command), and an upgrade guide for each minor version.
  • A designer guide: build a child style, use design tokens, override a template.
  • An admin guide that covers installation, upgrades, migration from each supported platform, performance tuning and security.
  • Machine-readable docs (llms.txt, JSON) so AI coding assistants give correct answers about vBulletin.


Roadmap

The work runs in five phases. Each one ships something usable, and each ends at a gate it must pass before the next begins. Phases 0 and 1 change nothing for add-on authors; the clean break happens in Phase 2.

Every phase ships something; 7.0 Final ships only after the release gate
Phases in order, each ending at a gate it must pass. Not drawn to a time scale.

Phase 0 · 6.2.x security update
  • Replace or patch CKEditor 4.13; remove Facebook SDK 4.0.9 and the dead APC cache; update Stripe
  • Build the benchmark data set and record 6.2.x baseline numbers
  • Write and agree the RFCs: extension manifest, contracts, events, template slots

◇ Gate: baseline measured, RFCs agreed

Phase 1 · 6.3 foundations (no breaking changes)
  • Unminified source; namespaces with class_alias for old names; Composer with a scoped vendor folder
  • DI container behind vB::getX(); bin/vb console for install, upgrade and cron
  • PHPUnit and PHPStan in CI; MyISAM tables to InnoDB; time columns widened past 2038

◇ Gate: 6.3 passes CI and upgrade tests with no regressions

Phase 2 · 7.0 alpha (the clean break)
  • Symfony-component kernel, extension system, typed events and template slots; zero eval()
  • Twig styles with the template converter; file-based languages; Default and Classic styles
  • New frontend and Tiptap editor on index, channel and thread pages; guest page cache

◇ Gate: the new core pages beat the 6.2 baseline on every metric

Phase 3 · 7.0 public beta
  • Blogs, groups, articles, calendar and albums as official extensions; REST API and webhooks
  • Importers from the most widely used forum platforms; batched CLI upgrade rehearsed on real boards
  • 15+ extensions from us and early-access developers; external security audit

◆ Release gate: feature parity with 6.x and every target in Goals met

Phase 4 · 7.0 Final, then 7.x
  • Real-time updates; more importers; Meilisearch and OpenSearch search extensions
  • ActivityPub federation, optional AI tools, marketplace and extension catalogue growth
  • 6.x security-only from 7.0 beta; end of support 18 months after 7.0 Final


The release gate before 7.0 Final is the most important line in this plan: no date pressure moves it.

Durations are deliberately not estimated here. They depend on team size and on what the Phase 0 benchmark shows. Once the team agrees the scope, each phase gets a dated plan.

Risks and mitigations

The biggest risk is repeating vB5: a long, ambitious rewrite that ships late, slower and with fewer features than the version it replaces. Most mitigations below exist to prevent exactly that.
Risk Impact Mitigation
Scope grows and 7.0 slips for years Customers leave while they wait; team morale drops Phased plan where every phase ships something. Fixed release gate. Features that miss a phase move to 7.x, not into a bigger 7.0
7.0 ships slower or with fewer features than 6.x Repeat of vB5, lasting brand damage Benchmark in CI from day one; parity checklist; long public beta; Final only when the gate passes
Custom styles break on upgrade Admins refuse to upgrade Twig converter with a report; Classic style; conversion help for large customers during beta
Add-on catalogue empty at launch "Nothing works on v7" 15+ extensions at launch; early-access developer programme; porting support
Team too small for the full plan Everything half-done Prioritise by phase (Roadmap). The slim core reduces what must be rewritten. Official extensions can follow after 7.0
Shared hosting can't run queues, Redis or CLI Features fail on cheap hosts Every advanced piece has a fallback: DB queue drained by requests and cron, DB or filesystem cache, browser installer and upgrader
Large boards can't upgrade in an acceptable window Big customers stay on 6.x Batched migrations, resumable CLI upgrade, dry run, rehearsal on customer copies during beta
Symfony major versions force churn Ongoing maintenance cost Track LTS releases only; dependencies scoped so extensions are isolated from our upgrade timing
Security regression in new code Loss of trust PHPStan, composer audit, CSP, external audit before Final, public security policy
Maintaining 6.x and 7.x together drains the team Both suffer 6.x moves to security-only fixes once 7.0 enters beta; a published end-of-support date for 6.x
Decisions needed

These decisions shape the plan and are the team's or leadership's to make. Each comes with this proposal's recommendation.
  • ☐ Template engine. Twig in 7.0, or keep {vb:...} file-based for 7.0 and move later? Recommendation: Twig in 7.0, since the clean break is happening anyway.
  • ☐ Minimum PHP version. 8.3 or 8.4? Recommendation: 8.3, checked against hosting statistics before beta.
  • ☐ Editor. Tiptap, or another modern editor? Recommendation: Tiptap, plus an interim CKEditor fix in 6.2.x.
  • ☐ Upgrade floor. Is 5.7.x / 6.x as the direct upgrade source acceptable? Recommendation: yes, with older sites going through 6.2 first.
  • ☐ Which features become official extensions (Slim core table): confirm or adjust the list.
  • ☐ Release cadence after 7.0. Recommendation: a minor release every 8 to 10 weeks, security releases as needed.
  • ☐ 6.x end of support. Recommendation: security-only from 7.0 beta, end of support 18 months after 7.0 Final.


Immediate next steps
  1. Review this proposal as a team and record decisions on the list above.
  2. Ship the 6.2.x security update (editor, Facebook SDK, Stripe, APC removal).
  3. Build the benchmark data set and capture 6.2.x baseline numbers for the release gate.
  4. Write the first RFCs: the extension manifest and contracts, the event list, and the template slot list.
  5. Build the Phase 1 proof of concept: the new kernel serving the index, channel and thread pages from Twig, measured against the 6.2.x baseline.
